pages.x: In April 1792 revolutionary France declared war on Austria, home of the French queen, Marie Antoinette. Prussia joined Austria, and its commander warned that Paris would be destroyed if the royal family were harmed. Instead, the threat helped to topple the king.

That April an army officer, Rouget de Lisle, wrote a war song for the Army of the Rhine in Strasbourg. Volunteers from Marseille sang it as they marched into Paris that summer, and it took their name. In 1795 it became the national anthem of France.

On 20 September 1792, at Valmy, the raw volunteers of the new French army stood firm under Prussian cannon fire, shouting long live the nation, and the Prussians turned back. The next day France became a republic. The German poet Goethe, who was there, said that a new age of history had begun.

In 1793, with enemies on every border and revolts at home, the Republic ordered the levée en masse: every unmarried man from 18 to 25 was called up, and everyone else had a task, from making weapons to tearing old linen into bandages. France raised armies of about 800,000, the largest Europe had ever seen.

In 1796 a 26-year-old general, Napoleon Bonaparte, took command of a hungry, ragged army in Italy. In a year of lightning marches he beat the Austrians again and again, at Lodi, Arcole and Rivoli, and forced them to make peace. He sent home gold, and paintings and statues taken from Italy's churches and palaces.

In 1798 Bonaparte sailed to Egypt, to strike at Britain's route to India. He beat the Mamluks in sight of the pyramids, but Admiral Nelson destroyed his fleet at the Battle of the Nile, trapping his army. Scholars who came with him studied Egypt's past, and his soldiers found the Rosetta Stone, the key to reading hieroglyphs.

Bonaparte slipped back to France in 1799 and seized power as First Consul. In 1800 he crossed the Alps and beat the Austrians at Marengo, while another French army won at Hohenlinden. Austria made peace, and in 1802 even Britain signed the Peace of Amiens. It lasted fourteen months.

The wars carried the ideas of the Revolution, equality before the law and the nation as the source of power, across Europe, along with French armies and looting. They made Napoleon, and led straight into his wars. The nation in arms became the model for the wars of the next 150 years.
